short: China’s political upheaval of 1966–1976.
note: A mass political campaign launched by Mao Zedong in 1966, attacking supposed bourgeois influences and political enemies. It disrupted education, government, and cultural life throughout China.

short: Chinese Communist revolutionary and leader, 1893–1976.
note: A founder of the People’s Republic of China and its dominant political leader from 1949 until his death in 1976. His campaigns included the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution.

sources.label: Columbia University: Mao and the Cultural Revolution

short: Large handwritten posters for public political messages.
note: Chinese dazibao: wall posters bearing large handwritten characters, used to broadcast accusations, arguments, and political demands. They became a prominent instrument of the Cultural Revolution.

short: Rural institutions for political reeducation through labor.
note: Institutions established during the Cultural Revolution to send officials and intellectuals into agricultural labor and political study. Their name referred to Mao’s directive of May 7, 1966.

sources.label: Chinese Posters: May Seventh Cadre Schools

short: Five politically stigmatized social categories in Maoist China.
note: Landlords, rich peasants, counterrevolutionaries, “bad elements,” and rightists: categories used to classify supposed class enemies and targets of political persecution.

sources.label: Chinese Posters: historical poster and catalog record

short: Urban young people sent to live and work in the countryside.
note: Educated urban youths dispatched to rural China under the “Up to the Mountains and Down to the Countryside” movement, especially from 1968 onward, for labor and political reeducation.

sources.label: Chinese Posters: Up to the Mountains

short: The December 1978 meeting associated with China’s reform era.
note: The Third Plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s Eleventh Central Committee marked a political shift toward economic development and reform under Deng Xiaoping.

sources.label: Columbia University: Deng Xiaoping and reform

short: Chinese novelist and playwright, 1899–1966.
note: The pen name of Shu Qingchun, a novelist and dramatist known for portrayals of life in Beijing. He taught Chinese at the School of Oriental Studies in London during the 1920s.

short: Chinese writer and literary scholar, 1910–1998.
note: A Chinese writer and scholar of comparative literature who studied at Oxford in the 1930s. His work draws on both Chinese and European literary traditions.

sources.label: University of Oxford: China and Oxford

short: Chinese geophysicist and pioneer of satellite research.
note: A geophysicist who helped establish China’s atmospheric and space-science research and advocated the development of an artificial-satellite program in the 1950s.

sources.label: Chinese Academy of Sciences: early space research

short: Chinese writer and founding president of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
note: A writer and scholar who became the first president of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. His 1978 address “The Spring of Science” welcomed a renewal of scientific research.

sources.label: Chinese Academy of Sciences: The Spring of Science

short: Canadian physician who served in wartime China.
note: A Canadian surgeon, 1890–1939, who organized medical care for Chinese Communist forces during the war against Japan. Mao Zedong’s memorial essay made him a celebrated example of international solidarity.

short: American marine biologist and environmental writer.
note: An American biologist, 1907–1964, whose 1962 book Silent Spring documented environmental damage from pesticides and helped change public attitudes toward chemical pollution.

sources.label: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: institutional history

short: Rachel Carson’s influential 1962 book on pesticides.
note: A study of the ecological consequences of indiscriminate pesticide use, especially DDT. Its account of harm to birds and other wildlife helped stimulate the modern environmental movement.

sources.label: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: Rachel Carson

short: The first emperor of a unified China.
note: The ruler of Qin who unified China in 221 BCE and took the title First Emperor. His immense funerary complex near Xi’an includes the terracotta army.

sources.label: UNESCO: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

short: A legendary culture hero associated with cosmic order.
note: A primordial Chinese culture hero, often paired with Nüwa. Traditional accounts connect him with the ordering of civilization and the invention of the eight trigrams used in divination.

short: Ancient Chinese philosopher and founder of Mohism.
note: Mo Di, or “Master Mo,” was a fifth-century BCE Chinese thinker. Mohism advocated impartial concern for others, practical benefit, frugality, and opposition to aggressive warfare.

short: The era of competing Chinese kingdoms before unification.
note: The period extending from the fifth century to 221 BCE, when rival Chinese states fought for supremacy and major philosophical schools developed. It ended with Qin’s unification of China.

short: Radical youth groups mobilized during the Cultural Revolution.
note: Student and youth organizations that rallied to Mao Zedong’s Cultural Revolution from 1966. They attacked perceived political enemies, authority figures, and remnants of traditional culture.

sources.label: UK National Archives: Cultural Revolution source pack

short: The pocket collection of Mao Zedong’s quotations.
note: Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, widely issued in small red-bound editions. It became a central object of political study and public ritual during the Cultural Revolution.

sources.label: UK National Archives: Cultural Revolution source pack

short: Chinese teacher and philosopher, traditionally 551–479 BCE.
note: Kongzi, or “Master Kong,” whose teachings concern ethical cultivation, humane government, family relationships, and ritual. The Analects preserves sayings and dialogues associated with him and his disciples.

short: The Chinese Book of Changes, a classic of divination and philosophy.
note: A text organized around sixty-four hexagrams, each composed of six broken or unbroken lines. Its accumulated interpretations link changing configurations with judgments about conduct, circumstances, and cosmic order.

short: The Zhou ruler traditionally associated with the Book of Changes.
note: An eleventh-century BCE Zhou ruler traditionally credited with statements interpreting the I Ching’s hexagrams. The text’s historical authorship is more complex than this traditional attribution.

short: Six-line figures used in the I Ching.
note: The sixty-four combinations of six broken or unbroken lines in the Chinese Book of Changes. Each figure has associated statements used in divination and philosophical interpretation.

short: Complementary, interacting aspects of Chinese cosmology.
note: Paired tendencies associated with contrasts such as shade and light, rest and activity, and yielding and firmness. Their interaction expresses transformation rather than a simple opposition of good and evil.

short: Chinese translator and writer, 1908–1966.
note: A Chinese literary translator and critic, particularly known for translating French literature. His work helped introduce writers such as Balzac to Chinese readers.

short: Chinese historian associated with Tsinghua University.
note: A historian of imperial China who taught at Tsinghua University and became one of the prominent scholars associated with its history department.

short: Chinese historian and academic leader at Peking University.
note: A historian of China who helped develop Peking University’s history department, supporting work in archaeology, world history, and the study of classical texts.

short: Ye Yiqun, a Chinese writer and literary critic.
note: Ye Yiqun, 1911–1966, was a writer associated with Shanghai’s literary institutions and served as deputy director of the Shanghai Film Studio. He died during the Cultural Revolution.

sources.label: University of Chicago: Cultural Revolution victims archive

short: Chinese poet, 1923–1971.
note: A poet from the Zhenjiang area of Jiangsu, remembered for poetry depicting the lives and landscapes of China’s frontier regions.

short: Greek philosopher and investigator of nature, 384–322 BCE.
note: A student of Plato whose writings cover logic, ethics, politics, biology, physics, and metaphysics. His explanations of nature profoundly influenced later Greek, Islamic, and European scholarship.

short: Possibly Tao Qian’s account of a secluded, peaceful community.
note: Possibly Tao Qian’s classical prose work in which a fisherman discovers a hidden settlement whose inhabitants live beyond the wars and political upheavals of the outside world.

short: A device that amplifies microwaves by stimulated emission.
note: An acronym for microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. A maser produces or amplifies coherent microwave radiation; hydrogen masers also serve as highly stable frequency standards.

short: Philosopher associated with animal ethics.
note: An Australian philosopher whose 1975 book Animal Liberation argues that the interests and suffering of nonhuman animals deserve serious moral consideration.

short: Peter Singer’s influential 1975 work on animal ethics.
note: A philosophical argument against disregarding animal suffering merely because the beings affected belong to other species. It examines practices including intensive farming and animal experimentation.

short: The 1997 international agreement on greenhouse-gas emissions.
note: An agreement under the United Nations climate convention that established emissions commitments for industrialized countries and economies in transition. Adopted in 1997, it entered into force in 2005.

short: The United Nations’ 1948 statement of fundamental human rights.
note: A declaration adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1948, setting out universal civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights.

sources.label: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

short: China’s Cold War program of industrial construction in the interior.
note: A major program begun in the 1960s to build strategic industries in inland China, especially the southwest and west, as a protected reserve against possible war.

short: The last ruler of the Shang dynasty.
note: Di Xin, remembered as King Zhou in later Chinese tradition, was the final Shang king. His defeat by the Zhou in the eleventh century BCE ended the Shang dynasty.

term: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
short: Zhang Zeduan’s famous Northern Song handscroll.
note: An early twelfth-century Chinese painting filled with densely observed figures, boats, buildings, and everyday urban activity. The original handscroll is held by the Palace Museum in Beijing.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum Journal: Zhang Zeduan’s handscroll

short: The artificial waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
note: A ship canal across the Isthmus of Panama. Locks raise vessels from sea level to an inland lake system and lower them again on the opposite coast.

sources.label: Panama Canal Authority: design of the locks

short: The two-step locks near the Pacific end of the Panama Canal.
note: A pair of successive lock chambers that raises or lowers vessels between the Pacific approach and Miraflores Lake in the original Panama Canal system.

sources.label: Panama Canal Authority: design of the locks

short: Predicting the motion of three mutually gravitating bodies.
note: The problem of finding how three bodies move under their mutual gravitational attraction. Many configurations are chaotic and require numerical methods; special exact or periodic solutions also exist.

sources.label: American Museum of Natural History: the three-body problem

short: English mathematician and physicist, 1643–1727.
note: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, developed a form of calculus, and made major discoveries in optics. His Principia appeared in 1687.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Isaac Newton

short: Mathematician and pioneer of modern computing.
note: John von Neumann, 1903–1957, made foundational contributions to mathematics, quantum theory, game theory, and computing. The stored-program computer architecture commonly named after him keeps instructions and data in memory.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: John von Neumann

short: Astronomer who placed the Sun at the center of the planetary system.
note: Nicolaus Copernicus, 1473–1543, developed a mathematical model in which Earth rotates and the planets orbit the Sun. His major work, De revolutionibus, was published in 1543.

short: Experimental physicist who demonstrated parity violation.
note: Chien-Shiung Wu, 1912–1997, led the experiment showing that weak nuclear interactions do not always behave identically to their mirror images, overturning the assumed conservation of parity.

short: Radio astronomer who helped discover the cosmic microwave background.
note: Arno Penzias, 1933–2024, and Robert Wilson detected the cosmic microwave background in the 1960s. Their discovery supplied crucial evidence for a hot early universe and earned them the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics.

short: Mathematician known for work on the three-body problem.
note: An American mathematician who, with Alain Chenciner, proved the existence of a periodic figure-eight orbit in which three equal masses follow the same curve under Newtonian gravity.

sources.label: Annals of Mathematics: Chenciner and Montgomery, 2000

short: Mathematician who helped establish the figure-eight three-body orbit.
note: A French mathematician whose work with Richard Montgomery demonstrated a periodic solution for three equal masses chasing one another around a figure-eight path under Newtonian gravity.

sources.label: Annals of Mathematics: Chenciner and Montgomery, 2000

short: The distance inside which tidal forces can disrupt an orbiting body.
note: A boundary within which a larger body’s tidal forces can overcome the self-gravity holding a smaller body together. The distance depends on density and on the smaller body’s physical strength.

short: The cooled radiation left over from the early universe.
note: Microwave radiation arriving from all directions, released when the early universe became transparent roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Its tiny temperature variations record the seeds of later cosmic structure.

short: NASA’s Cosmic Background Explorer satellite.
note: A satellite launched in 1989 to measure the universe’s diffuse background radiation. It established the nearly perfect thermal spectrum of the cosmic microwave background and detected small temperature variations across the sky.

short: NASA’s Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe.
note: A space mission that mapped small temperature differences in the cosmic microwave background, allowing precise estimates of the universe’s age, composition, and early structure.

sources.label: NASA: WMAP and the cosmic microwave background

short: The European Space Agency’s cosmic-background observatory.
note: A space telescope launched in 2009 to map the cosmic microwave background with high sensitivity and angular resolution. It refined measurements of the universe’s composition and early history.

short: An early radio search for extraterrestrial intelligence.
note: Frank Drake’s 1960 experiment at Green Bank, using a radio telescope to listen toward Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani near the 21-centimeter hydrogen wavelength.

sources.label: Green Bank Observatory: the Tatel telescope

short: A nearby Sun-like star targeted by early SETI searches.
note: A star in the constellation Cetus, chosen along with Epsilon Eridani for Frank Drake’s Project Ozma radio search in 1960.

short: A nearby star targeted by Project Ozma.
note: A star in the constellation Eridanus, observed with Tau Ceti in the pioneering 1960 radio search for extraterrestrial intelligence at Green Bank.

short: A major radio-astronomy site in West Virginia.
note: The observatory site where Frank Drake conducted Project Ozma in 1960 using the 85-foot Howard E. Tatel telescope.

short: Quantum correlations between parts of a shared physical state.
note: A relationship in which the quantum state of a combined system cannot be described as independent states of its parts. Entanglement produces strong correlations, but cannot transmit usable information faster than light.

short: The force binding quarks and holding atomic nuclei together.
note: One of the fundamental interactions, mediated by gluons between quarks. Its residual effects bind protons and neutrons into nuclei and act over extremely short distances.

short: Physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity.
note: Albert Einstein, 1879–1955, transformed ideas about space, time, gravity, and light. His explanation of the photoelectric effect earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

short: Italian pioneer of experimental physics and telescopic astronomy.
note: Galileo Galilei, 1564–1642, investigated motion and used telescopes to reveal lunar mountains, Jupiter’s moons, and other evidence challenging inherited views of the heavens.

short: Mathematician who founded cybernetics.
note: An American mathematician, 1894–1964, who studied probability, communication, feedback, and control. His 1948 book Cybernetics connected the regulation of machines with processes in living organisms.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Norbert Wiener

short: French mathematician who pioneered the study of dynamical systems.
note: Henri Poincaré, 1854–1912, made fundamental contributions to topology and celestial mechanics. His work on the three-body problem revealed behavior central to the later development of chaos theory.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Poincaré biography

short: Renaissance philosopher who argued for an infinite universe.
note: An Italian philosopher, 1548–1600, who proposed an infinite cosmos containing innumerable worlds. His cosmology formed part of a wider metaphysical and religious system.

short: Astronomer who discovered Uranus in 1781.
note: William Herschel, 1738–1822, built powerful reflecting telescopes and discovered Uranus. His astronomical work was closely associated with that of his sister Caroline and later his son John.

sources.label: Royal Museums Greenwich: the Herschel family

short: Astronomer whose laws describe planetary orbits.
note: Johannes Kepler, 1571–1630, established that planets follow elliptical orbits, sweep out equal areas in equal times, and obey a mathematical relationship between orbital period and distance from the Sun.

short: Marie Curie, a pioneering researcher on radioactivity.
note: Marie Skłodowska Curie, 1867–1934, helped discover polonium and radium. She received Nobel Prizes in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.

sources.label: Nobel Prize: the Curies and radioactivity

short: A family of interpretations of quantum mechanics.
note: Views associated with Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg, and their colleagues that emphasize measurement, probabilistic outcomes, and the limits of classical descriptions of atomic phenomena. The label covers differing positions rather than one agreed doctrine.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Copenhagen interpretation

short: The physical theory of atomic and subatomic systems.
note: A framework that predicts physical outcomes using quantum states and probabilities. Features such as discrete energy levels, interference, and entanglement distinguish it from classical mechanics.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: quantum mechanics

short: A mathematical description of a quantum state.
note: A function whose amplitudes allow the probabilities of measurement outcomes to be calculated. Its evolution and interpretation are central questions in quantum mechanics.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: quantum states

short: Materials with structures on the scale of billionths of a meter.
note: Materials whose features are approximately 1–100 nanometers across. At this scale, physical and chemical properties can differ substantially from those of the same substance in bulk.

short: Einstein’s theory of space, time, and motion without gravity.
note: The theory in which observers moving uniformly relative to one another agree on the speed of light in vacuum but can disagree about lengths, elapsed times, and which distant events are simultaneous.

short: The constant linking a photon’s energy with its frequency.
note: The constant h in the relation E = hν. Introduced by Max Planck in the study of thermal radiation, it sets the scale of quantum effects and has units of energy multiplied by time.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: origins of quantum theory

short: The relationship between voltage, current, and electrical resistance.
note: For an ohmic conductor under fixed physical conditions, current is proportional to applied voltage: V = IR. The law is named for the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm.

short: A family of numerical methods based on random sampling.
note: Methods that estimate mathematical or physical quantities by generating random samples and analyzing their statistical behavior. They are especially useful when direct calculation would be impractical.

short: The nearest stellar system to the Sun.
note: A nearby triple-star system in Centaurus, consisting of the close pair Alpha Centauri A and B and the more distant red dwarf Proxima Centauri. The bright pair lies about 4.3 light-years away.

short: Relatively cool, magnetically active patches on the Sun.
note: Dark-looking regions of the Sun’s visible surface where strong magnetic fields inhibit the usual transport of heat. They are cooler than their surroundings, rather than empty holes.

short: The Puerto Rican observatory famous for its giant radio telescope.
note: A radio-astronomy and radar research site whose 305-meter reflector began operating in 1963. The dish was built into a natural depression in the landscape.

short: The equations unifying electricity and magnetism.
note: Four equations relating electric and magnetic fields to charges, currents, and changes in one another. James Clerk Maxwell’s formulation showed that light is an electromagnetic wave.

short: Understanding and controlling matter at nanometer scales.
note: Research and engineering involving structures approximately 1–100 nanometers across, where size-dependent properties enable materials and devices to behave differently from their larger counterparts.

short: Einstein’s theory of gravity as the geometry of spacetime.
note: A theory in which mass and energy affect the curvature of spacetime, and that geometry governs the paths of freely moving bodies and light.

sources.label: Max Planck Institute: Einstein’s geometric gravity

short: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence.
note: Scientific searches for observable evidence of technology beyond Earth, including artificial radio signals, laser pulses, and other potential technological signatures.

short: A straight-line alignment of celestial bodies.
note: An alignment of three celestial bodies, as when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up at a full or new moon. Exact alignment can produce an eclipse.

short: A traditional Chinese plucked zither.
note: A long, bridged zither played by plucking strings with the right hand and bending or pressing them with the left. Modern instruments commonly have twenty-one strings.

sources.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art: guzheng

short: Simon Browne’s hymn asking the Holy Spirit for guidance.
note: An eighteenth-century Christian hymn by Simon Browne, published in 1720. It addresses the Holy Spirit as a heavenly dove and asks for comfort, guidance, and a path toward holiness.
A branched stand holding several candles.
short: A branched candleholder.
Fine, floating spider silk; something extremely light and delicate.
note: The thin threads of spider silk that float through the air or cling to vegetation. By extension, gossamer describes filmy fabric or anything exceptionally fine, light, or insubstantial.

short: A table of celestial positions at specified times.
note: An astronomical table giving the calculated positions of a planet, Moon, or other celestial body at successive times. The plural is ephemerides.

short: A shoulder belt for carrying ammunition.
note: A belt worn diagonally across the chest, with loops or pouches for cartridges or other equipment.

short: A draped garment worn in ancient Greece.
note: A tunic-like garment of ancient Greece, usually reaching the knees on men and the feet on women.

short: An alloy of copper and nickel.
note: A metal alloy combining copper with nickel.

short: Ring-shaped models of the heavens.
note: Astronomical instruments made from rings representing important circles of the celestial sphere, such as the equator and ecliptic.

short: An instrument for detecting ionizing radiation.
note: A detector in which radiation ionizes gas inside a tube, producing electrical pulses that can be counted and displayed or heard.

short: A constructed language for international communication.
note: An international auxiliary language devised by L. L. Zamenhof, drawing much of its vocabulary from European languages.

short: A frequency shift caused by relative motion.
note: The change in observed frequency when a wave source and observer move relative to one another. Approaching light shifts toward blue; receding light shifts toward red.

short: A member of the Russian revolutionary Communist faction.
note: A member of the faction of the Russian Social Democratic movement that seized power in 1917.

short: Medieval architecture characterized by rounded arches.
note: A western European architectural style preceding Gothic, associated especially with rounded arches, vaulting, substantial piers, and arcades.

short: A one-sided surface formed by a half-twisted band.
note: A strip joined end to end after giving it a half-turn. It has one continuous side and one boundary edge.

short: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, philosopher and mathematician.
note: The German polymath (1646–1716) developed infinitesimal calculus and mechanical calculating machines.

sources.label: Leibniz University Hannover: life and work

short: A coil that acts as an electromagnet.
note: A coil of wire, usually cylindrical, that produces a magnetic field when current passes through it; such coils can operate mechanical switches and valves.

short: A statement that does not logically follow.
note: Latin for “it does not follow”: an inference unsupported by its premises, or a remark disconnected from what preceded it.

short: The sky imagined as a great overarching vault.
note: A literary word for the heavens or apparent arch of the sky.

short: The Roman-letter spelling system for Mandarin Chinese.
note: A system for writing Chinese pronunciation with the Latin alphabet, using accent marks to indicate tones.

short: A heated masonry sleeping platform.
note: A brick platform traditionally used for sleeping in northern Chinese homes, warmed by a fire or hot flue gases beneath it.

short: Doughnut-shaped surfaces or bodies.
note: The plural of torus: a ring-shaped surface made by revolving a circle around an axis outside it.

short: Loud electric warning horns.
note: Electrically operated horns or alarms. Klaxon was originally a trademark.

short: A pale mineral carved into tobacco pipes.
note: A light, whitish hydrous magnesium silicate, prized as a material for carving tobacco-pipe bowls.

short: A vacuum tube that generates microwaves.
note: An electronic tube in which a magnetic field controls moving electrons to produce microwave-frequency power.

short: Particles composed of a quark and an antiquark.
note: A class of subatomic particles, including pions and kaons, that participate in the strong interaction. A conventional meson contains a quark–antiquark pair.

short: An instrument that displays an electrical waveform.
note: An instrument that turns changes in an electrical signal into a visible trace on a screen, allowing its waveform to be examined.

short: Having age-related difficulty focusing on nearby objects.
note: Affected by presbyopia, the loss of close-focusing ability caused by reduced flexibility of the eye’s lens with age.

short: A closely packed formation of troops.
note: Originally a dense, ordered formation of ancient Greek infantry; more broadly, any massed body arranged in close ranks.

short: Able to hold molecules on a surface.
note: An adsorbent collects molecules in a thin layer on its surface; adsorption concerns surface attachment rather than penetration throughout the material.

short: Stout posts used to secure mooring ropes.
note: Strong posts on a ship or wharf around which ropes are fastened to hold a vessel in place.

short: Lightweight rifles with relatively short barrels.
note: Compact rifles developed for easier handling, historically associated with cavalry.

short: A Latin title for a foremost ruler or leader.
note: Latin for one who is first; historically a title of the head of the Roman imperial state.

short: Below the range of human hearing.
note: Describes sound or vibration with a frequency lower than the human ear can normally hear.

short: Matter made from the antiparticles of ordinary particles.
note: Antiparticles have the same masses as their corresponding particles but opposite electric charges where charged. Matter and antimatter can annihilate on contact, releasing energy.

short: The maximum ship size for the original Panama Canal locks.
note: A ship-size standard determined by the dimensions of the Panama Canal’s original lock system; the later enlarged locks admit the larger Neopanamax class.

sources.label: Panama Canal Authority: original and expanded locks

short: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.
note: An immersed body experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid or gas it displaces. Named for the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes.

short: More distant galaxies generally recede faster.
note: The relationship linking a galaxy’s recession speed to its distance: on cosmological scales, recession speed is proportional to distance, with the Hubble constant as the proportionality factor.

sources.label: NASA: Hubble constant and cosmic expansion

short: Combining widely separated radio telescopes.
note: A technique that combines precisely timed observations from distant antennas to obtain much finer angular detail than a single dish can resolve. Abbreviated VLBI.

sources.label: National Radio Astronomy Observatory: radio-astronomy FAQ

short: The geometry of Euclid’s postulates.
note: The classical geometry of lines, planes, and solids developed from the axioms and postulates of Euclid’s Elements, including the parallel postulate.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Euclid and the Elements

short: Renaissance artist, engineer, and scientific investigator.
note: Leonardo (1452–1519) combined painting and sculpture with studies of anatomy, geometry, machinery, and flight. His paintings include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

short: Johann Sebastian Bach, composer and organist.
note: The German composer (1685–1750), long based in Leipzig, wrote music for voices, orchestra, organ, and other keyboard instruments.

short: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, composer from Salzburg.
note: The composer (1756–1791) was a celebrated childhood performer who later worked in Vienna; his output includes operas, symphonies, concertos, and chamber music.

short: Ernest Hemingway, noted for economical prose.
note: A twentieth-century American writer whose unadorned sentences and understated dialogue often leave important meaning implicit rather than explicitly explained.

sources.label: US National Endowment for the Arts: Hemingway’s writing style

short: ACM’s leading award in computing.
note: The Association for Computing Machinery’s prestigious technical award, often compared with a Nobel Prize for computing.

sources.label: Association for Computing Machinery: Turing Award anniversary

short: The first emperor of a unified China.
note: The ruler of Qin who unified China in 221 BCE and took the title First Emperor. His immense funerary complex near Xi’an includes the terracotta army.

sources.label: UNESCO: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

short: Ancient Chinese philosopher and founder of Mohism.
note: Mo Di, or “Master Mo,” was a fifth-century BCE Chinese thinker. Mohism advocated impartial concern for others, practical benefit, frugality, and opposition to aggressive warfare.

short: Chinese teacher and philosopher, traditionally 551–479 BCE.
note: Kongzi, or “Master Kong,” whose teachings concern ethical cultivation, humane government, family relationships, and ritual. The Analects preserves sayings and dialogues associated with him and his disciples.

short: A pendulum that demonstrates the Earth’s rotation.
note: A freely swinging pendulum whose plane of swing changes relative to the rotating Earth. The United Nations’ gold-plated example was presented by the Netherlands in 1955.

term: Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares
short: A United Nations sculpture based on Isaiah’s image of peace.
note: Evgeniy Vuchetich’s bronze of a man hammering a sword into a farming tool, given to the United Nations by the Soviet Union in 1959. Its title echoes the biblical Book of Isaiah.

sources.label: United Nations: Let Us Beat Swords Into Ploughshares

short: The 1982 war over the Falkland Islands.
note: The conflict between Argentina and the United Kingdom after Argentine forces occupied the Falkland Islands, called the Islas Malvinas in Spanish. It ended in June 1982 with the surrender of Argentine forces.

sources.label: U.S. Department of State: South Atlantic crisis

short: An oasis on the Silk Road near the Mogao Buddhist caves.
note: An oasis town in Gansu, northwestern China, associated with the nearby Mogao cave temples and their paintings, sculptures, and extraordinary manuscript collections.

sources.label: British Library: Silk Roads exhibition guide

short: The Daoist caretaker who rediscovered Dunhuang’s Library Cave.
note: A Daoist priest caring for the Mogao caves who uncovered their sealed manuscript chamber in 1900. He later sold portions of its contents to foreign researchers including Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot.

short: The Zhou ruler traditionally associated with the Book of Changes.
note: An eleventh-century BCE Zhou ruler traditionally credited with statements interpreting the I Ching’s hexagrams. The text’s historical authorship is more complex than this traditional attribution.

short: The Chinese Communist leadership’s headquarters before Beijing.
note: A village in Hebei where the Communist Party’s central leadership was based in 1948–1949, directing the final major campaigns of the Chinese Civil War.

sources.label: China.org.cn: Xibaipo museum and historic site

short: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait of Lisa Gherardini.
note: A Renaissance portrait of Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del Giocondo, painted by Leonardo da Vinci. The painting is also known as La Gioconda and is held by the Louvre.

short: Greek philosopher and investigator of nature, 384–322 BCE.
note: A student of Plato whose writings cover logic, ethics, politics, biology, physics, and metaphysics. His explanations of nature profoundly influenced later Greek, Islamic, and European scholarship.

short: Possibly the Ming admiral who led seven great overseas expeditions.
note: Possibly Zheng He, the Chinese admiral whose fleets sailed through the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, reaching ports as far away as the east coast of Africa.

short: Hangzhou’s celebrated lake and cultural landscape.
note: A lake bordered by Hangzhou and wooded hills, shaped over centuries with causeways, islands, temples, pagodas, and gardens. Its idealized scenery profoundly influenced East Asian landscape design.

short: A Hindu scripture framed as Krishna’s counsel to Arjuna.
note: The “Song of the Lord,” a section of the Mahabharata in which Krishna addresses Arjuna’s doubts before battle. It explores duty, action, knowledge, devotion, and liberation.

sources.label: Harvard Divinity Bulletin: the Bhagavad Gita

short: The Qing dynasty’s northern modernized naval force.
note: A late-Qing naval force based partly at Liugong Island near Weihaiwei. Its defeats in the First Sino-Japanese War exposed the limits of China’s nineteenth-century military modernization.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Through Wind and Rain

short: Qing naval officer and captain of the battleship Dingyuan.
note: The captain of the Beiyang Fleet’s flagship Dingyuan during the First Sino-Japanese War. After the ship was damaged at Weihaiwei in 1895, he ordered it scuttled and took his own life.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Dingyuan

short: The 1895 battle that ended the Beiyang Fleet’s resistance.
note: A Japanese land and naval operation against the Qing naval base at Weihaiwei during the First Sino-Japanese War. Capture of the coastal forts and attacks on the ships led to the fleet’s defeat.

sources.label: Hong Kong Museum of History: Weihaiwei

short: A museum preserving records of Japanese wartime suicide pilots.
note: A museum in Chiran, Kagoshima, associated with the army airbase used for special-attack missions during the Battle of Okinawa. Its collection includes pilots’ letters, photographs, and personal effects.

short: Leader of South American independence from Spain.
note: A military and political leader who helped defeat Spanish rule in northern South America and became president of the republic commonly called Gran Colombia.

sources.label: Library of Congress: the 1821 Colombian constitution

short: The early republic uniting much of northern South America.
note: The republic that encompassed present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama after independence from Spain. Its union broke apart around 1830.

short: The artificial waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
note: A ship canal across the Isthmus of Panama. Locks raise vessels from sea level to an inland lake system and lower them again on the opposite coast.

sources.label: Panama Canal Authority: design of the locks

short: Founder of the Mongol Empire, circa 1162–1227.
note: The Mongol ruler whose conquests established an empire that his successors extended across much of Eurasia. Its successor states included the Yuan dynasty in China and the Ilkhanate in Iran.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum: The Legacy of Genghis Khan

short: Predicting the motion of three mutually gravitating bodies.
note: The problem of finding how three bodies move under their mutual gravitational attraction. Many configurations are chaotic and require numerical methods; special exact or periodic solutions also exist.

sources.label: American Museum of Natural History: the three-body problem

short: English mathematician and physicist, 1643–1727.
note: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, developed a form of calculus, and made major discoveries in optics. His Principia appeared in 1687.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Isaac Newton

short: Mathematician and pioneer of modern computing.
note: John von Neumann, 1903–1957, made foundational contributions to mathematics, quantum theory, game theory, and computing. The stored-program computer architecture commonly named after him keeps instructions and data in memory.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: John von Neumann

short: Five special positions in a two-body orbital system.
note: Positions where a small object can remain in a fixed configuration relative to two larger orbiting bodies. L1, L2, and L3 are unstable; L4 and L5 can be stable when the larger bodies’ mass ratio is sufficiently unequal.

short: The broad region of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
note: A disk-like region beyond Neptune containing Pluto and many other icy bodies left from the Solar System’s formation. It is a major source of short-period comets.

short: A proposed distant reservoir of icy bodies around the Solar System.
note: A vast, roughly spherical population of icy bodies inferred from the paths of long-period comets. It is thought to extend far beyond the planets and the Kuiper Belt.

short: Quantum correlations between parts of a shared physical state.
note: A relationship in which the quantum state of a combined system cannot be described as independent states of its parts. Entanglement produces strong correlations, but cannot transmit usable information faster than light.

short: The joining of light atomic nuclei, releasing energy.
note: A nuclear reaction in which light nuclei combine into heavier ones. Fusion powers stars; energy is released when the products have less total mass than the starting particles.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy: fusion reactions

short: Hydrogen with one neutron in its nucleus.
note: A stable isotope of hydrogen whose nucleus contains one proton and one neutron. It occurs naturally in water and is one of the fuels studied for fusion energy.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy: deuterium–tritium fuel

short: Radioactive hydrogen with two neutrons in its nucleus.
note: An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons. Fusion of tritium with deuterium produces a helium nucleus and an energetic neutron.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy: deuterium–tritium fuel

short: A doughnut-shaped magnetic device for confining hot plasma.
note: A fusion-research device that combines external magnetic fields with an electric current in the plasma to confine it within a toroidal chamber. The name comes from a Russian abbreviation.

short: The force binding quarks and holding atomic nuclei together.
note: One of the fundamental interactions, mediated by gluons between quarks. Its residual effects bind protons and neutrons into nuclei and act over extremely short distances.

short: Physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity.
note: Albert Einstein, 1879–1955, transformed ideas about space, time, gravity, and light. His explanation of the photoelectric effect earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

short: The physical theory of atomic and subatomic systems.
note: A framework that predicts physical outcomes using quantum states and probabilities. Features such as discrete energy levels, interference, and entanglement distinguish it from classical mechanics.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: quantum mechanics

short: The observed growth of transistor counts on integrated circuits.
note: Gordon Moore’s projection that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit would approximately double every two years, as revised in 1975. It describes an industrial trend, not a physical law.

short: The apparent tension between possible abundant alien life and its absence from view.
note: The question associated with Enrico Fermi’s “Where is everybody?”: if technological civilizations can arise and spread through an ancient galaxy, why is there no convincing evidence of their presence?

short: Physicist who led the first controlled nuclear chain reaction.
note: An Italian-American physicist whose team achieved a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1 on December 2, 1942, opening the era of nuclear reactors.

short: Astronomer and influential communicator of science, 1934–1996.
note: A planetary scientist at Cornell University whose research and public writing concerned the Solar System, the possibility of extraterrestrial life, and the value of scientific reasoning.

short: Relatively cool, magnetically active patches on the Sun.
note: Dark-looking regions of the Sun’s visible surface where strong magnetic fields inhibit the usual transport of heat. They are cooler than their surroundings, rather than empty holes.

short: The continuous outflow of charged particles from the Sun.
note: A stream of plasma escaping the Sun’s outer atmosphere and flowing through the Solar System, carrying the Sun’s magnetic field with it.

short: Yoshiki Tanaka’s Japanese space-opera series.
note: A series of novels about interstellar war and political rivalry, contrasting an autocratic empire with a democratic alliance. Its central military figures include Reinhard von Lohengramm and Yang Wen-li.

sources.label: VIZ: Legend of the Galactic Heroes

short: Isaac Asimov’s series about the rise and fall of a galactic civilization.
note: A science-fiction sequence in which mathematician Hari Seldon develops psychohistory, a fictional statistical science of mass human behavior, and plans to shorten a coming age of social collapse.

short: Arthur C. Clarke and Stanley Kubrick’s space-exploration story.
note: The title of Clarke’s 1968 novel and Kubrick’s film, developed together. Both concern human evolution, mysterious extraterrestrial artifacts, and a voyage involving the computer HAL 9000.

sources.label: Penguin Random House: 2001: A Space Odyssey

short: British science-fiction writer, 1917–2008.
note: The author of Childhood’s End, 2001: A Space Odyssey, and Rendezvous with Rama, whose fiction and essays often concern spaceflight, advanced technology, and encounters with other forms of intelligence.

sources.label: Penguin Random House: Arthur C. Clarke

short: An ancient Greek philosophical dialogue on justice and government.
note: Plato’s dialogue explores justice in individuals and in an imagined city, the education of rulers, knowledge and appearance, and the relationship between political order and the soul.

short: A celebrated Hellenistic statue of a goddess.
note: An ancient Greek marble statue found on the island of Melos in 1820, usually identified as Aphrodite. It entered the Louvre in 1821 and is famous for its missing arms.

short: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, an ancient Greek sculpture.
note: A marble image of Nike, the goddess of victory, standing on a ship-shaped base. Discovered on Samothrace in 1863, it became one of the Louvre’s best-known sculptures.

short: A Russian song whose title means “Slender Rowan.”
note: A song based on Aleksey Koltsov’s poem about a solitary rowan tree longing to cross a river and join an oak. Ryabina means rowan or mountain ash.

short: Chinese novelist and essayist, author of Golden Age.
note: A Chinese writer known for satirical fiction that treats political conformity, sexuality, and individual freedom. His Golden Age sequence includes work set during and after the Cultural Revolution.

short: Anthony Burgess’s novel about violence, conditioning, and moral choice.
note: A 1962 novel narrated in an invented slang called Nadsat. It examines whether enforced behavioral conditioning can produce goodness while depriving a person of the capacity to choose.

sources.label: International Anthony Burgess Foundation: A Clockwork Orange

short: The 1215 English charter limiting royal authority.
note: A charter sealed by King John at Runnymede in June 1215 after conflict with his barons. Its lasting significance includes the principle that the ruler is subject to law.

short: The second Secretary-General of the United Nations.
note: A Swedish diplomat who led the United Nations from 1953 until his death in a plane crash during a peace mission in Africa in 1961.

short: Latin: seize the day.
note: Latin for seize the day, from Horace’s Odes 1.11. The phrase urges enjoyment of the present instead of reliance on an unknowable future.
A tall, four-sided stone pillar that tapers toward a small pyramidal top.
short: A tall stone pillar tapering to a pyramid.
The Dog Star, the brightest star in Earth’s night sky.
note: Sirius, the Dog Star in Canis Major, is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. It is a binary system: the brilliant Sirius A has a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B.

sources.label: NASA · Sirius, the brightest star in the night

short: Fine, floating spider silk; something extremely light and delicate.
note: The thin threads of spider silk that float through the air or cling to vegetation. By extension, gossamer describes filmy fabric or anything exceptionally fine, light, or insubstantial.

short: The sky imagined as a great overarching vault.
note: A literary word for the heavens or apparent arch of the sky.

short: A stony meteorite lacking chondrules.
note: A stony meteorite lacking the small rounded grains called chondrules; achondrites include rocks from differentiated asteroids, Mars, and the Moon.

sources.label: Natural History Museum: types of meteorites

short: An iron meteorite with intergrown crystalline plates.
note: A type of iron meteorite whose structure contains plates of kamacite intergrown with taenite, producing a distinctive crosshatched pattern.

short: An iron meteorite without a visible patterned structure.
note: A structural class of iron meteorites lacking the characteristic coarse structure of hexahedrites or octahedrites.

short: An iron–nickel mineral common in meteorites.
note: A natural alloy of iron and nickel which, together with taenite, makes up much of meteoritic iron.

short: An iron–nickel mineral found in meteoritic metal.
note: A natural iron–nickel alloy associated with kamacite in the metallic parts of many meteorites.

short: Interlocking crystal patterns in iron meteorites.
note: Crosshatched crystalline structures exposed by cutting and etching some iron meteorites. They develop as the iron–nickel metal cools extremely slowly.

sources.label: Natural History Museum: types of meteorites

short: Fine bands produced by shock in meteoritic iron.
note: Bands caused by twinning of the crystal structure in kamacite. Such deformation can record ancient impacts experienced by an iron meteorite.

sources.label: Ohtani and colleagues: experimental study of Neumann bands

short: Conventionally, Earth’s orbital reference plane.
note: Conventionally, the plane containing Earth’s orbit around the Sun, used as a reference for celestial positions and orbital inclinations.

short: Orbiting once per rotation of Earth.
note: Describes an Earth orbit with a period of one sidereal day, matching Earth’s rotation relative to the stars.

short: Ornamental shoulder pieces on a uniform.
note: Decorative strips or pads worn on the shoulders of clothing, especially military uniforms.

short: The upper edge of a boat’s side.
note: The top rim of the side of a boat or ship; traditionally pronounced “gunnel.”

short: A nearly massless, electrically neutral particle.
note: An elementary particle with a very small mass and no electric charge, which interacts only rarely with other matter.

short: A propagating ripple in spacetime.
note: A travelling disturbance of the gravitational field: a ripple in spacetime that carries energy away from its source.

short: Cosmic observations are conditioned by observers’ existence.
note: In its weak form, the principle notes that conditions we observe must permit observers to exist. Stronger forms make more controversial claims about life’s necessity.

short: Historical Japanese ritual suicide.
note: A form of ritual suicide historically associated with the Japanese samurai, also called hara-kiri.

short: Pleasure in another person’s misfortune.
note: A German loanword for enjoyment at another person’s troubles, formed from words meaning damage and joy.

short: A mixture of disparate things.
note: A mixture or assortment, often combining incongruous elements; the word comes from French.

short: The visible, light-emitting layer of a star.
note: The luminous surface layer of the Sun or another star, from which most of its visible light emerges.

short: Kenneth Bainbridge, director of the Trinity test.
note: The American physicist (1904–1996) who directed preparations for Trinity, the first atomic-bomb test, carried out in New Mexico in July 1945.

sources.label: US National Park Service: Kenneth Bainbridge

short: The physicist who directed wartime Los Alamos.
note: J. Robert Oppenheimer led the Los Alamos laboratory during the Manhattan Project, coordinating the scientific work that produced the first atomic bombs.

sources.label: US National Park Service: Oppenheimer and the Manhattan Project

short: Alfred Thayer Mahan, theorist of naval power.
note: The American naval historian argued that control of the seas, merchant shipping, and overseas bases were central to national power. His influential The Influence of Sea Power upon History appeared in 1890.

sources.label: US Office of the Historian: Mahan and sea power

short: A story by Alphonse Daudet about comforting deception.
note: In Daudet’s story, an ill French veteran is shielded from news of military defeat through invented reports of French victories.

sources.label: Wikisource: Alphonse Daudet, The Siege of Berlin

short: Below the range of human hearing.
note: Describes sound or vibration with a frequency lower than the human ear can normally hear.

short: Imaging an object’s internal cross sections.
note: A method of reconstructing internal structure from measurements taken through an object, often producing sectional or three-dimensional images.

short: Ordinary hydrogen with a mass number of one.
note: The lightest and most common isotope of hydrogen, with a nucleus consisting of a single proton and no neutron.

short: A large sail for travelling with the wind.
note: A broad triangular sail spread outward from a light pole, used when a sailing vessel runs before the wind.

short: Matter made from the antiparticles of ordinary particles.
note: Antiparticles have the same masses as their corresponding particles but opposite electric charges where charged. Matter and antimatter can annihilate on contact, releasing energy.

short: A prehistoric stone-circle monument in southern England.
note: A monument built in stages, with its great stone circle erected around 2500 BCE. Its standing stones form part of a much larger prehistoric landscape.

short: The grinning cat in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.
note: Lewis Carroll’s cat can disappear while leaving its grin visible after the rest of its body has gone.

sources.label: Wikisource: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, chapter 6

short: The traveller in Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels.
note: In the giant land of Brobdingnag, Gulliver observes skin at an enlarged scale and finds apparently smooth beauty rough and uneven close up.

sources.label: Project Gutenberg: Gulliver’s Travels, Part II

short: Wolfgang Becker’s 2003 film about an elaborate deception.
note: A young man protects his mother after she wakes from a coma by pretending that East Germany still exists, recreating familiar surroundings and news broadcasts.

sources.label: British Film Institute: Good Bye, Lenin!

short: A primordial creator figure in Chinese mythology.
note: Also written P’an Ku. In creation myths he separates heaven from earth; in some versions the features of the world arise from his body.

sources.label: Columbia University: four versions of the P’an Ku myth

short: Fear or aversion to the sun.
note: A word formed from Greek-derived elements meaning sun and fear.

short: Psychologist associated with psychedelic research and counterculture.
note: An American psychologist (1920–1996) who studied mind-altering drugs at Harvard and later became a prominent figure in the psychedelic and human-potential movements.

sources.label: Harvard Department of Psychology: Timothy Leary

short: The ancient Greek mathematician associated with the Elements.
note: Euclid of Alexandria organized geometry into a deductive system in the Elements, beginning from definitions, postulates, and common notions.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Euclid biography

short: The geometry of Euclid’s postulates.
note: The classical geometry of lines, planes, and solids developed from the axioms and postulates of Euclid’s Elements, including the parallel postulate.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Euclid and the Elements

short: Nikolai Gogol, author of The Overcoat.
note: Gogol’s The Overcoat, also translated as The Mantle, portrays an impoverished copying clerk, Akaky Akakievich, subjected to the petty cruelties of official life.

short: Pluto’s largest moon.
note: Charon is about half Pluto’s diameter. The two bodies are mutually tidally locked, so each always presents the same face to the other.

short: A large, heavily cratered moon of Jupiter.
note: The second-largest Jovian moon and the third-largest moon in the Solar System, discovered with the other Galilean satellites in 1610.

short: Jupiter’s icy moon with evidence of a subsurface ocean.
note: One of the Galilean moons of Jupiter. Its icy surface overlies a likely saltwater ocean, making it an important target for investigating potentially habitable environments.

short: The dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt.
note: The largest body in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, classified as a dwarf planet. It contains substantial water-bearing material.

short: An astronomical unit, roughly 150 million kilometres.
note: A distance unit approximately equal to Earth’s average distance from the Sun, often used for dimensions and distances within a planetary system.

short: Charles Darwin, theorist of evolution by natural selection.
note: The naturalist explained how inherited variation and differences in survival and reproduction can gradually alter species. His 1857 abstract outlines natural selection and the divergence of living forms.

sources.label: University of Cambridge: Darwin’s abstract of his theory

short: The last Byzantine emperor.
note: Constantine XI Palaiologos was the last Byzantine emperor. His reign ended with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453.

short: The Byzantine capital, now Istanbul.
note: The city now called Istanbul was the capital of the Byzantine Empire and later the Ottoman Empire. It fell to the forces of Mehmed II in 1453.

short: The Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople.
note: Mehmed II, known as the Conqueror, captured Constantinople in 1453 and made it an Ottoman capital. He also supported scholarship, art, and major building projects.

short: George Sphrantzes, Byzantine diplomat and chronicler.
note: George Sphrantzes served the last Byzantine emperors as a court official and diplomat. His Chronicon Minus records his personal and political life during the fifteenth century.

short: The sixth-century Church of Holy Wisdom in Istanbul.
note: Hagia Sophia, Greek for Holy Wisdom, was built in Constantinople in 532–537 under Justinian I. Its vast dome became a landmark of Byzantine architecture; the building later served as a mosque.

short: The fifth-century Eastern Roman emperor associated with Constantinople’s land walls.
note: Theodosius II was the Eastern Roman emperor under whom Constantinople’s great land defenses took shape. The expanded fifth-century fortifications are known as the Theodosian Walls.

short: Kafka’s short story of a father’s sentence against his son.
note: Franz Kafka wrote The Judgment, originally Das Urteil, in a single night in September 1912; it first appeared in 1913. Its young protagonist receives an impossible-seeming condemnation from his father.

short: Turgenev’s prose poem about accepting sacrifice.
note: Ivan Turgenev’s prose poem The Threshold presents a young woman who accepts suffering and condemnation as the price of crossing into a life of committed action.

sources.label: Ivan Panin: Lectures on Russian Literature, including The Threshold

short: Ron Jones’s 1967 classroom demonstration of authoritarian conformity.
note: In 1967, California teacher Ron Jones organized a classroom movement called the Third Wave to demonstrate the appeal of authoritarian discipline and group loyalty. Participants’ accounts differ on some details.

sources.label: The Wave: original participants’ history and FAQ

short: A Song poet associated with the lyric of lovers separated along a river.
note: Li Zhiyi was a Song-dynasty poet active in the late eleventh century. His lyric to the tune Busuanzi describes lovers living far apart while sharing the water of the same river.

sources.label: Macao Cultural Affairs Bureau: Li Zhiyi and Busuanzi

term: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
short: Zhang Zeduan’s panoramic Song-dynasty handscroll.
note: An early-twelfth-century handscroll by Zhang Zeduan depicting the crowded streets, waterways, and everyday activity of the Northern Song capital. Its composition inspired many later copies and reinterpretations.

sources.label: National Palace Museum: Up the River During Qingming

short: Poe’s tale of a survivor of a Norwegian whirlpool.
note: Edgar Allan Poe’s A Descent into the Maelström recounts a fisherman’s terrifying encounter with an immense Norwegian whirlpool. The survivor studies the motions of floating objects to find a way out.

sources.label: Poe Museum: A Descent into the Maelström

short: A powerful tidal current in Norway’s Lofoten archipelago.
note: The Moskstraumen is a strong tidal current and whirlpool system near Moskenes in the Lofoten Islands of northern Norway. It supplied the setting for Poe’s A Descent into the Maelström.

short: Latin: seize the day.
note: Latin for seize the day, from Horace’s Odes 1.11. The phrase urges enjoyment of the present instead of reliance on an unknowable future.

short: An undeciphered Bronze Age writing system of Crete.
note: A script used in Bronze Age Crete before the Greek-writing Linear B. Linear A has not been securely deciphered, and the language it records remains unidentified.

sources.label: Oxford classical reference entries: pre-Greek languages

short: An undeciphered script of Bronze Age Crete.
note: A pictorial writing system of Bronze Age Crete, distinct from Egyptian hieroglyphs and from the later Greek-writing Linear B. The language behind its signs is not securely identified.

sources.label: Oxford classical reference entries: pre-Greek languages

short: Lishu, a form of Chinese writing developed for scribal use.
note: Clerical script, or lishu, evolved in the late first millennium BCE and became widely used under the Han dynasty. Its flattened forms and distinctive spreading strokes became important models for later calligraphy.

short: Van Gogh’s 1889 painting of a turbulent night sky.
note: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night at Saint-Rémy in June 1889. Its swirling blue sky, bright celestial bodies, village, and dark cypress combine observation with an imaginative reconstruction of the view.

sources.label: Museum of Modern Art: The Starry Night

short: The English essayist whose Of Boldness tells the mountain-and-Muhammad anecdote.
note: Francis Bacon’s essay Of Boldness tells an anecdote in which Muhammad, unable to make a mountain approach, decides to go to it. It is a literary anecdote in Bacon, rather than an authenticated episode from Muhammad’s life.

short: A theoretical physicist known for work on gravitation and cosmology.
note: Charles W. Misner (1932–2023) was a theoretical physicist and a major contributor to general relativity. He coauthored Gravitation and helped develop the Arnowitt–Deser–Misner formulation of Einstein’s theory.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Charles W. Misner

short: A natural time unit of about 5.39 × 10⁻⁴⁴ seconds.
note: The natural unit of time formed from the reduced Planck constant, the gravitational constant, and the speed of light: √(ℏG/c⁵), approximately 5.39 × 10⁻⁴⁴ seconds.

short: The event-horizon radius of an uncharged, nonrotating black hole.
note: The radius 2GM/c² for a mass M, where G is the gravitational constant and c the speed of light. It gives the event-horizon radius of an ideal nonrotating, uncharged black hole.

sources.label: NASA Imagine the Universe: black holes

short: The seismic boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.
note: The boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle, detected through a marked change in seismic-wave speed. Often shortened to Moho, it is named for the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić.

sources.label: USGS: Seismic velocity structure of the continental lithosphere

short: A dense, olivine-rich rock characteristic of the upper mantle.
note: A dark, dense rock rich in the mineral olivine. Peridotite makes up much of Earth’s upper mantle beneath the crust.

short: A mathematician who studied propulsion by repeated nuclear explosions.
note: Stanislaw Ulam worked on mathematics, computing, and nuclear physics at Los Alamos. With Cornelius Everett, he investigated propelling a spacecraft with a sequence of external nuclear explosions, an idea later associated with Project Orion.

short: A proposed drive powered by successive nuclear explosions.
note: A proposed method of accelerating a spacecraft through repeated nuclear explosions outside the vehicle. Ulam and Everett studied the concept at Los Alamos; it later formed the basis of Project Orion.

short: Hypothetical structures that collect a star’s energy.
note: Hypothetical engineering on a stellar scale: structures or swarms of collectors arranged around a star to capture its energy. Their waste heat could produce excess infrared radiation detectable from afar.

short: The broad region of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
note: A thick belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune, including Pluto and many other remnants of the early Solar System. Its principal region extends roughly from 30 to 50 astronomical units from the Sun.

short: The proposed distant reservoir of icy comet bodies around the Solar System.
note: A vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies inferred to surround the Solar System far beyond the Kuiper Belt. It is thought to supply many long-period comets.

short: One of five places where a small body can keep its position relative to two orbiting masses.
note: In an ideal two-body orbital system, one of five locations where a third, small body can move with the other two while retaining its relative position. At Sun–Earth L1, gravity provides the acceleration needed for the shared orbital period.

short: A small moon of Jupiter, named for the mythological mother of Helen.
note: A small member of Jupiter’s Himalia group of moons, discovered in 1974. Its name comes from Leda, whom Zeus visited in the form of a swan in Greek mythology.

short: The joint mission to Saturn and its moon Titan.
note: Launched in 1997, the NASA–ESA–ASI mission combined the Cassini Saturn orbiter with ESA’s Huygens probe. Huygens landed on Titan in January 2005; Cassini studied Saturn until 2017.

short: The Soviet space shuttle that flew in 1988.
note: The Soviet winged spacecraft carried into orbit by the Energia launcher. Buran made its only spaceflight in November 1988.

sources.label: ESA: Fifty Years of Access to Space

short: An image of imminent danger hanging over apparent good fortune.
note: In the ancient anecdote, Damocles enjoys a ruler’s luxurious seat until he notices a sword suspended above him by a single horsehair. The image represents the insecurity that accompanies power and prosperity.

sources.label: Perseus: Horace commentary citing Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.61

short: A three-script decree that helped unlock Egyptian hieroglyphs.
note: A stone decree issued in 196 BCE under Ptolemy V, written in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Egyptian demotic, and Greek. Comparing its parallel versions helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphic writing.

short: Dazhuan, the older forms of Chinese seal writing.
note: Also called large-seal script or dazhuan: early Chinese character forms associated especially with inscriptions on Shang and Zhou ritual bronzes. These precede the more standardized small-seal script.

sources.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art: Seal Script

short: Xiaozhuan, the standardized seal writing of the Qin period.
note: Chinese seal writing standardized under the Qin dynasty, with balanced forms and relatively even lines. It was used for official inscriptions and remained influential in later seal carving and calligraphy.

sources.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art: Seal Script

short: The Shijing, an ancient Chinese anthology of songs and poems.
note: The Shijing, also called the Book of Odes, is an ancient collection of more than three hundred Chinese poems. Its songs, court odes, and hymns became central texts of the Confucian tradition.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum: Courtly Odes, Beginning with Wild Geese

short: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait of Lisa Gherardini.
note: Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait of Lisa Gherardini, the wife of Francesco del Giocondo, also known as La Gioconda. Its softly shaded face and elusive smile are celebrated examples of his sfumato technique.

short: The Paris monument and burial place honoring distinguished figures.
note: A monumental building in Paris whose crypt became a national burial place during the French Revolution. Among those commemorated there are Voltaire and Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

sources.label: Centre des monuments nationaux: Panthéon guide

short: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the philosopher of The Social Contract.
note: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was the Genevan philosopher whose Social Contract argued for sovereignty grounded in the people. His remains were transferred to the Paris Panthéon in 1794.

sources.label: Centre des monuments nationaux: Panthéon guide

short: An Aboriginal Australian poet and playwright.
note: A Western Australian poet, dramatist, and advocate for Aboriginal people. His publications include the poetry collection The First Born and the plays No Sugar and The Dreamers.

sources.label: State Library of Western Australia: Jack Davis

short: An Aboriginal Australian wind instrument with a deep drone.
note: A long wind instrument originating in northern Australia, traditionally made from naturally hollowed wood. The player vibrates the lips at one end to produce its characteristic sustained drone.

short: A sacred Chinese mountain associated with imperial ceremonies.
note: Mount Tai, or Taishan, is one of China’s traditionally sacred mountains. Emperors performed rites there honoring Heaven and Earth; its temples, inscriptions, and landscape carry a long religious and literary history.

short: A sacred Buddhist mountain in Sichuan.
note: Emeishan, in Sichuan, is a major center of Chinese Buddhist pilgrimage. Temples are set among forests that range from subtropical vegetation to high-altitude conifers.

short: The great Giza pyramid built as the tomb of Khufu.
note: The largest pyramid at Giza, built for the Egyptian king Khufu, called Cheops in Greek. Originally about 146.5 metres high, it is the surviving monument of the ancient Seven Wonders.

sources.label: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities: The Great Pyramid

short: The French heroine condemned in 1431 and exonerated in 1456.
note: Joan of Arc, also called the Maid of Orléans, became a central figure of French resistance during the Hundred Years’ War. She was tried and burned at Rouen in 1431; a later trial cleared her in 1456.

short: The 1959 agreement reserving Antarctica for peaceful activity and scientific cooperation.
note: Signed in 1959 and in force from 1961, this treaty sets Antarctica aside for peaceful purposes and supports freedom of scientific investigation. It preserves the parties’ positions on territorial claims without allowing new claims while it remains in force.

short: The 1982 international convention governing uses of the seas.
note: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea was concluded at Montego Bay in 1982 and entered into force in 1994. It establishes a framework for maritime zones, navigation, ocean resources, and protection of the marine environment.

sources.label: United Nations Treaty Collection: Convention on the Law of the Sea

short: The celebrated armless Greek statue of Aphrodite.
note: A Hellenistic Greek marble statue generally identified as Aphrodite, the goddess called Venus by the Romans. Discovered on the island of Melos in 1820, it is famous for its missing arms and now belongs to the Louvre.

short: The Civil War romance centered on Scarlett O’Hara and Tara.
note: Margaret Mitchell’s story, adapted as the 1939 film, follows Scarlett O’Hara from plantation life in Georgia through the American Civil War and Reconstruction. Tara is her family’s plantation.

sources.label: Library of Congress: Gone with the Wind

short: Like the one-eyed giants of Greek mythology.
note: From the Cyclopes, giants of Greek mythology. The best-known is Polyphemus, whose single eye Odysseus blinds in Homer’s Odyssey. The adjective can suggest a single enormous eye or gigantic scale.

sources.label: Theoi: Polyphemus, with ancient source texts

short: The sixth-century Byzantine emperor associated with Hagia Sophia and Roman-law codification.
note: Justinian I ruled the Byzantine Empire from 527 to 565. His reign included reconquests around the Mediterranean, the codification of Roman law, and construction of the present Hagia Sophia.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum: The Byzantine State under Justinian I

short: A tune pattern used for Chinese ci lyrics.
note: A named tune pattern, or cipai, used in Chinese ci poetry. Such patterns prescribe the arrangement of lines, tones, and rhymes; different poets supply their own words to the same form.

sources.label: Shandong University: Study of short ci tune patterns

short: The popular religious expeditions of 1212, remembered for their young participants.
note: A name given to popular crusading movements in France and Germany in 1212, involving many young people who hoped to reach Jerusalem. Contemporary accounts are fragmentary, and later stories about their fate are difficult to verify.

sources.label: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook: Chronicle account of 1212

short: An early Chinese design for a multistage naval rocket.
note: Chinese for fire-dragon emerging from the water. The name refers to an early gunpowder-rocket design for naval warfare, with an outer rocket carrying smaller projectiles—a precursor in concept to staged rockets.

sources.label: China National Space Administration: Early Chinese rockets

short: The historical cannon-founder also called Urban.
note: A fifteenth-century cannon-founder, also known as Urban, associated with the enormous Ottoman bombards used against Constantinople in 1453. He worked for Sultan Mehmed II.

sources.label: Edward Gibbon: Decline and Fall, chapter 68
Cambridge University Press: Guns for the Sultan, index

short: The era of competing Chinese kingdoms before unification.
note: The period extending from the fifth century to 221 BCE, when rival Chinese states fought for supremacy and major philosophical schools developed. It ended with Qin’s unification of China.

short: Possibly Isaac Newton, the English physicist and mathematician.
note: Possibly Isaac Newton (1643–1727), who formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, developed calculus, and made major discoveries in optics.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Isaac Newton

short: Quantum correlations between parts of a shared physical state.
note: A relationship in which the quantum state of a combined system cannot be described as independent states of its parts. Entanglement produces strong correlations, but cannot transmit usable information faster than light.

short: The force binding quarks and holding atomic nuclei together.
note: One of the fundamental interactions, mediated by gluons between quarks. Its residual effects bind protons and neutrons into nuclei and act over extremely short distances.

short: Physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity.
note: Albert Einstein, 1879–1955, transformed ideas about space, time, gravity, and light. His explanation of the photoelectric effect earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

short: Materials with structures on the scale of billionths of a meter.
note: Materials whose features are approximately 1–100 nanometers across. At this scale, physical and chemical properties can differ substantially from those of the same substance in bulk.

short: Einstein’s theory of space, time, and motion without gravity.
note: The theory in which observers moving uniformly relative to one another agree on the speed of light in vacuum but can disagree about lengths, elapsed times, and which distant events are simultaneous.

short: The joining of light atomic nuclei, releasing energy.
note: A nuclear reaction in which light nuclei combine into heavier ones. Fusion powers stars; energy is released when the products have less total mass than the starting particles.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy: fusion reactions

short: A doughnut-shaped magnetic device for confining hot plasma.
note: A fusion-research device that combines external magnetic fields with an electric current in the plasma to confine it within a toroidal chamber. The name comes from a Russian abbreviation.

short: The continuous outflow of charged particles from the Sun.
note: A stream of plasma escaping the Sun’s outer atmosphere and flowing through the Solar System, carrying the Sun’s magnetic field with it.
A branched stand holding several candles.
short: A branched candleholder.
The Dog Star, the brightest star in Earth’s night sky.
note: Sirius, the Dog Star in Canis Major, is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. It is a binary system: the brilliant Sirius A has a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B.

sources.label: NASA · Sirius, the brightest star in the night

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.
A small boat carried by, or serving, a larger ship.
short: A small boat used with a larger vessel.

note: A stone coffin, often carved or decorated.
short: A stone coffin.
Danish astronomer whose observations helped establish Kepler’s laws.
note: Tycho Brahe, 1546–1601, made exceptionally precise observations of stars and planets before the telescope. Johannes Kepler used his measurements to develop the laws of planetary motion.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Tycho Brahe

short: Possibly an echo of Alfred Bester’s The Stars My Destination.
note: Possibly an echo of Alfred Bester’s science-fiction novel The Stars My Destination (1956), also published as Tiger! Tiger! It is a revenge narrative set in a future dominated by powerful corporations.

sources.label: Library of America: Five Classic Novels 1956–1958
Library of America: William Gibson on The Stars My Destination

short: A curved sword with one cutting edge.
note: A sword whose blade curves and has its cutting edge on the outer, convex side. The name is traditionally applied to several kinds of Middle Eastern and Asian swords.

short: Early cannon built to hurl heavy stone balls.
note: An early type of cannon, especially a heavy gun used against fortifications. Bombards originally fired stone balls rather than the iron projectiles associated with later artillery.

short: A shoulder belt for carrying ammunition.
note: A belt worn diagonally across the chest, with loops or pouches for cartridges or other equipment.

short: An instrument for detecting ionizing radiation.
note: A detector in which radiation ionizes gas inside a tube, producing electrical pulses that can be counted and displayed or heard.

short: A frequency shift caused by relative motion.
